title: Safety net and reversion playbook for production experiments
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a working playbook for cross-functional teams running production experiments (canaries, A/B tests, staged rollouts) that focuses on automated and human-triggered reversion, escalation, and safety nets. It is deliberately pragmatic: short checklists, concrete signal thresholds, sample automation commands, and templates for communications.

Scope / audience:
- Applies to experiments that route >0.5% of production traffic or affect critical user flows (auth, billing, billing webhooks, payments, embeddings used by search).
- Primary readers: product PMs, engineering leads, SRE/Oncall, Data/ML ops, Solutions Eng.

High-level principles (TL;DR):
- Prefer automated, safe, reversible mechanisms for fast containment.
- Always define primary guardrail metrics and a single, unambiguous stop condition before launch.
- Think in three layers: automated kill-switch, rapid human rollback, and traffic-remapping fallback.
- Keep comms templates ready so teams don't waste time composing messages during incidents.

Key definitions used here:
- Canary: small % of traffic to a new variant (e.g., 1–5%).
- A/B test: controlled split with metric comparisons; may be persistent for weeks.
- Reversion: action that returns traffic to the last known-good variant or route.
- Safety net: automated monitoring + action that prevents user-visible degradation.

Pre-launch checklist (must be completed and signed off by PM + Eng Lead):
- Experiment plan doc exists and links to this playbook.
- Owner and backup owner listed and reachable (Slack + pager).
- Primary guardrail metrics (1–3) and their expected ranges defined (e.g., error rate <0.5%, median latency delta < +50ms).
- Clear stop conditions with exact numeric thresholds and evaluation window (e.g., 95th latency > 500ms for 5m sustained).
- Rollback method chosen: automated revert, feature-flag off, or traffic remap.
- Smoke tests and synthetic transactions configured against the canary route.
- Observability: dashboards, alert rules, and playbook links created.
- Runbook visible to oncall and product in shared channel.

Guardrail metrics (examples and recommended thresholds) – adapt to workload:
- User-facing error rate: primary HTTP 5xx or model-level failures. Threshold: >0.5% absolute increase vs baseline for 3 minutes.
- Request latency (p50/p95): threshold: p95 increase > +30% relative to baseline for 5m.
- Quality regression (for ML): evaluation score drop > 2 percentage points on core evalset within daily retrain window.
- Cost spikes: request cost per minute > 2x expected burn for 10m.
- Resource saturation: GPU mem usage > 92% or queue depth > 8 sustained for 3m.

Automated safety nets (recommended stack):
- Signal collector -> rules engine -> action executor.
- Preferred actions in order: 1) circuit-break request routing (reduce canary to 0%); 2) fallback to compatible variant (model-v1 -> model-v1-quantized-fallback); 3) degrade features (disable streaming attachments); 4) escalate if unable to revert.

Sample automated action definitions (pseudo):
- rule "canary-error-rate" when: canary.error_rate > 0.005 for 3m then: action set_traffic(canary, 0%) notify(#prod-rollouts)
- rule "gpu-saturation" when: gpu.util > 0.92 for 5m then: action set_autoscale(burst=true) and set_traffic(canary, 0%)

Concrete reversion methods (ordered by speed and invasiveness):
1) Feature-flag toggle: turn off feature flag targeting canary cohort. (fast, low-risk if code guards are correct)
2) Traffic remap at edge/router: set canary weight to 0% and divert to stable pool.
3) Model variant fallback: automatic substitution to 'stable' model shim (compatible tokenization/version).
4) Full rollback of deployment (rare for tiny code-only flags).

Commands / API examples (ops-ready snippets):
- Remap traffic (router CLI):
  rtr update-split --route /api/generate --variant stable --weight 100 --auth-token $OPS_TOKEN

- Feature flag off (FF service):
  ffctl set user-targeting my-feature off --env prod --actor team-rollouts

Slack escalation template (post to #prod-rollouts and #oncall):
- Subject: [AUTO-REVERT] Canary remapped -> 0% for /api/generate
- Body: Canary route exceeded error-rate guardrail (0.82% over threshold). Automatic action: set_traffic(canary=0%). Owner: Ava Martinez (@ava). Pager: @sre-oncall. Next steps: investigate errors -> revert permanent?

Human rollback flow (when automation not triggered or incomplete):
- T+0m: Owner + oncall confirm metrics and reproduce with synthetic test.
- T+5m: If immediate impact persists, owner issues remap command and marks experiment paused.
- T+15m: Incident channel created, primary stakeholders notified, triage begins.
- T+60m: Either fix-and-resume or permanent revert decision; if revert, create follow-up ticket and postmortem.

Escalation matrix (quick):
- Severity P0 (data loss, payment failures, system-wide errors): SRE oncall -> Eng L2 -> Eng Director -> CTO. Everyone paged.
- Severity P1 (degraded UX for many users): SRE oncall -> Owner (PM) -> Eng Lead. Pager + Slack.
- Severity P2 (minor regression in metrics): Owner -> Eng Lead -> monitor. No pager unless escalated.

Post-action requirements (after any automated revert or human rollback):
- Immediately pin traffic to stable variant and mark experiment paused.
- Create a short incident note in the experiment doc: cause hypothesis, initial mitigation, who performed revert, timestamps.
- Run scheduled root cause analysis within 72h.
- If automated action triggered, preserve signal logs (at least 90 days) and attach to postmortem.

Quick checklist for postmortem doc (to fill in):
- What happened? One paragraph.
- When (timeline) and how discovered?
- Which guardrail fired and why (false positive vs true regression)?
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence.
- Corrective actions (short-term and long-term).
- Owner and due dates for fixes.

Operational caveats and common pitfalls:
- Too many guardrails with slightly different thresholds -> oscillation. Prefer 1 canonical stop condition per experiment.
- Alert fatigue: automated actions that are too sensitive will cause frequent rollbacks and hide real problems. Tune with a small burn-in.
- Cross-team confusion: pre-announce the experiment window and likely reversion behavior to all dependent teams (search, billing, notifications).
- Canary cohorts must be isolated in telemetry (tag events) so aggregation doesn't dilute signal.

Templates and artifacts to create before launch (copy-and-edit):
- Short experiment blurb for #prod-rollouts channel with schedule and owners.
- Slack escalation message (above).
- Synthetic smoke script and runbook snippet for quick reproduction.
- Automated rule definitions pushed to rules engine repo and code-reviewed.

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Decide canonical default thresholds for "user-facing error" per product vertical (search vs chat vs embeddings). Need metrics team input. (Assigned: Priya)
- Add example Terraform module for traffic remap (Ops infra). (Assigned: Marcus)
- Should automated reversion create a ticket automatically? Pros: traceability. Cons: noisy tickets. Quick poll with PMs. (Action: Liam)

Notes to self / fragments (informal):
- We should run a "canary chaos" day where we intentionally trigger automated revert for dummy experiments to exercise the human flows.
- Consider a lightweight badge in Console that shows experiment health (green/orange/red) pulled from guardrail engine.

Appendix: sample metric rule JSON (for rules engine ingestion) — minimal example:
{
  "name": "canary_high_5xx",
  "scope": "/api/generate",
  "condition": "p(5xx_rate,3m) > 0.005",
  "action": "set_traffic(canary,0)",
  "notify": ["#prod-rollouts"]
}

Last edited by: Ava Martinez. Please test automation in staging and link the staging artifact here before attempting prod rollout.
